usage: I'll take the hot one, please.
Customer to barista; standard polite when picking hot over iced
반말 to a friend behind the counter or a very casual setting; rarely said to staff
거로 and 걸로 are both fine; 걸로 (걸=거+ㄹ) is the everyday spoken form
Natural extension: name the drink instead of just 'the hot one'
examples: A: 따뜻한 거 드릴까요, 아이스요? / B: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요.
A: Shall I make it hot, or iced? / B: Hot, please.
걸로 directly answers a binary hot/iced question — the particle -(으)로 signals 'I'm choosing this option'
라떼 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. 시럽은 빼고요.
A hot latte, please. No syrup.
Adding a tweak right after the order: 빼고요 = 'leave it out'; -고요 softens any tacked-on request at a café counter
밖이 너무 추워서요, 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. 큰 사이즈로요.
It's freezing outside, so a hot one please. Large size.
Real spoken flow: optional reason ending in -서요 → temperature choice → size tweak, all politely chained
nuance: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요 is the standard answer when a barista asks 따뜻한 거요 아이스요? (hot or iced?) or when you order a hot drink unprompted. The particle -(으)로 attaches to the thing you're selecting and means 'I'll go with the ~'; 걸로 is simply 거(것) + 로 in spoken contraction, so '따뜻한 걸로' = 'the warm one.' Register is plain polite -요, which is correct for all café and store staff — never drop to 반말 (따뜻한 거 줘) with someone you don't know personally. The closest loanword alternative is 핫으로 주세요, understood by most younger baristas but 따뜻한 걸로 is the natural native default and carries no ambiguity. The critical English-speaker error is confusing 따뜻한 with 뜨거운: 뜨거운 describes something dangerously, painfully hot (a 뜨거운 냄비 = scorching pot), while 따뜻한 means pleasantly warm — using 뜨거운 걸로 at a café is technically intelligible but sounds as if you want to scald yourself.

structuredNuance.t: Word-by-word: 따뜻한(warm) + 걸(것을, the thing) + 로(choice particle, 'going with') + 주세요(give me). The whole phrase compresses to 'please give me the warm one' — the -(으)로 particle is what signals a selection between options, making this the natural counter-answer to a hot/iced binary question.

Use at any café or convenience store to specify a hot drink, whether the staff asked or you're ordering unprompted. Always -요 polite with staff; 반말 form 따뜻한 거 줘 is only for a friend staffing a pop-up or someone you know well — never with a stranger behind a counter.

핫으로 주세요 (loanword 'hot') is popular at chains and understood everywhere, but 따뜻한 걸로 is the safe, age-neutral native choice. 따뜻하게 해 주세요 ('please make it warm') is an occasional alternative but sounds like a temperature tweak mid-drink, not an ordering phrase.
따뜻한 걸로 → 따뜻한 거로 (both correct; 걸로 is more fluent in speech) → 따뜻한 [음료명] 한 잔 주세요 (name the specific drink) → 아주 따뜻하게 해 주세요 (ask for extra-hot). Chain size and extras after: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요, 큰 사이즈로요.

The classic mistake is using 뜨거운 instead of 따뜻한. 뜨거운 = scaldingly hot (you'd yell 뜨거워! if you burned yourself). Warm drinks are 따뜻한. Asking for 뜨거운 걸로 at a café is understood but marks you as unnatural — and sounds like you want to damage your tongue.

mistakes: Saying 뜨거운 걸로 주세요 for a hot drink — 뜨거운 means scaldingly hot (burns); warm-temperature drinks are 따뜻한, so use 따뜻한 걸로.
Dropping 로 and saying 따뜻한 거 주세요 — understandable but the 걸로 form ('the ~ one') is what signals you're choosing between options; omitting -로 is grammatically loose.
Using English 'hot one please' word order as 하나 따뜻한 주세요 — Korean puts the modifier before the noun: 따뜻한 거 / 따뜻한 걸로, not a numeral first.

usage: Customer to barista; the universal way to ask for a cold drink
반말 among friends; not used toward staff
Native equivalent; slightly more formal/older-sounding than 아이스로
Extension: 'iced americano' is so common it's clipped to 아아 in texting slang
examples: A: 따뜻한 거요, 아이스요? / B: 아이스로 주세요.
A: Hot or iced? / B: Iced, please.
아이스 is a fixed loanword for cold drinks; -로 marks your choice — don't skip the particle
여름엔 무조건 아이스로 주세요. 얼음 많이요.
In summer, always make it iced. Lots of ice.
얼음 많이요 = 'extra ice'; a standalone noun + 요 turns into a polite addition without a full verb
A: 뭐로 드릴까요? / B: 저는 아이스로 주시고, 친구는 따뜻한 걸로 주세요.
A: What can I get you? / B: Iced for me, and hot for my friend.
Two orders in one breath; 주시고 links the first request to the second smoothly — natural at a busy counter
nuance: 아이스로 주세요 is how you order any cold drink at a Korean café — 아이스 is the English word 'ice' borrowed as an adjective and is far more commonly heard than the native 차가운 거. The particle -로 marks your selection ('I'm going with iced'). The pairing opponent is 따뜻한 걸로. The practical difference between 아이스로 and 차가운 걸로: 아이스로 is the default café lingo, while 차가운 걸로 sounds a touch older or is used in a convenience store for bottled drinks. Register is plain polite -요 for all staff; 반말 아이스로 줘 is friends-only. The English-speaker pitfall is ordering 얼음 주세요 ('give me ice') thinking that means 'iced drink' — it literally requests a cup of ice cubes; the temperature selection is 아이스로, and 얼음 is used only to adjust ice quantity (얼음 많이요 / 얼음 빼고요).

structuredNuance.t: 아이스 (loanword 'ice') + 로 (selection particle 'going with') + 주세요 (give me). The phrase means 'please give me the iced version' — it's a temperature-selection formula, not literally 'give me ice.'

Directed at café baristas and convenience store staff when choosing cold over hot. Always -요 polite toward staff; 반말 아이스로 줘 only with a friend. Works for any cold drink, from iced coffee to bubble tea.

차가운 걸로 주세요 is the fully native equivalent; 아이스로 is today's everyday café default. 콜드로 주세요 is rarer and slightly awkward. The dividing line between 아이스로 and 차가운 걸로 is register and context: 아이스로 is casual café speech; 차가운 걸로 sounds slightly formal or suits bottled drinks.
아이스로 → 아이스 [음료명] 주세요 (name the drink) → 아이스 아메리카노 = 아아 (texting abbreviation). Ice quantity: 얼음 많이요 / 얼음 적게요 / 얼음 빼고요 (no ice).
Ordering 얼음 주세요 to mean 'iced' is a classic mistake — that literally requests a cup of ice cubes. The cold-drink choice is 아이스로 주세요. 얼음 is useful only for adjusting the ice amount afterward.

mistakes: Saying 얼음으로 주세요 to mean 'iced' — that asks for ice as the item itself; the cold-drink selection is 아이스로 주세요.
Pronouncing 아이스 English-style and not adding the particle — Korean needs -로: 아이스로 (with -로) to mark it as your selection between two options.
Mixing 아이스 차가운 걸로 주세요 — redundant; pick one form: 아이스로 or 차가운 걸로, not both together.

usage: Staff to customer; the polite offer formula -ㄹ까요? with humble 드리다
반말 version; only a friend working the counter would say this
Which size would you like to go with?
A slightly more formal staff phrasing using -하시겠어요
As for size, which one shall I get you?
Extension with topic 는, common when listing options before asking
examples: A: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? / B: 작은 거로 주세요.
A: What size? / B: A small, please.
Answer with 작은/큰 거로; 드릴까요 is the staff side, 주세요 is your side — match the register: staff uses 드리다, you use 주다
A: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? / B: 제일 큰 걸로요.
A: What size? / B: The biggest one.
제일 큰 = 'the biggest'; a bare [size + 걸로요] is the most natural short answer, no full verb needed
A: 따뜻한 라떼요. / B: 네, 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? 레귤러랑 라지 있어요.
A: A hot latte. / B: Sure, what size would you like? We have regular and large.
Staff commonly follow the size question by naming available options — listen for the offered sizes before answering
nuance: This is a staff-to-customer line, so a learner mostly needs to recognize it fast and reply confidently. 어떻게 드릴까요? literally means 'how shall I give it to you?' — 드리다 is the humble form of 주다 ('give'), and -ㄹ까요? offers a service; together they are the polite service-formula heard in cafés, restaurants, and convenience stores everywhere. You reply with a size + 걸로: 작은 걸로요 / 큰 걸로요, or chain-store English sizes 톨/그란데/벤티. A slightly more formal staff variant is 어떤 사이즈로 하시겠어요? — same meaning, a notch stiffer. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 드릴까요 and mentally translating every word: just catch 사이즈 and respond with your size choice. A second trap is answering '미디엄' — many Korean cafés do not use a medium tier; they offer 작은/큰 or the Starbucks trio, so always listen for the options they name before deciding.

structuredNuance.t: 사이즈 (size) + 어떻게 (how) + 드릴까요 (shall I give you — humble). Literally: 'How shall I give the size to you?' — really: 'What size would you like?' It is a polite service question, not a philosophical one about method.

Staff address you in 존댓말 using the humble verb 드리다 — you are the honored customer. Your reply stays in plain polite -요: 작은 걸로요 / 큰 걸로요. Never try to match their humility level — that would be grammatically odd.
어떤 사이즈로 하시겠어요? is the more formal alternative. 어떻게 드릴까요? is warmer and conversational; 하시겠어요? sounds like a written menu or a formal restaurant. Both ask the same thing.
Your answer options: 작은 걸로요 (small) / 큰 걸로요 (large) / 레귤러로요 / 라지로요 / 톨로요 / 벤티로요. To specify further: 제일 작은 걸로요 (the smallest) / 중간 걸로요 (medium, if offered).

Two traps: (1) Freezing because 드릴까요 sounds complex — only the word 사이즈 matters; reply with a size. (2) Answering 미디엄 — many Korean cafés have no medium; they offer two sizes or the Starbucks trio, so always wait to hear the options first.

mistakes: Freezing because 드릴까요 sounds unfamiliar — it is just polite 'shall I give you'; catch the word 사이즈 and answer with your size choice.
Answering with bare 작은 사이즈 and no particle — the natural form is 작은 걸로(요) or 작은 거로(요), the -(으)로 particle marking your selection.
Saying 미디엄 expecting a medium — many cafés offer only 작은/큰 or 톨/그란데/벤티; always pick from the sizes the staff name.

usage: Customer asking staff to log loyalty/stamp points to their account
반말; only with a friend, never with cashier staff
Softer, more deferential variant using 부탁드리다 (I humbly request)
Can I earn points here too?
Extension: asking first whether the store runs a points program at all
examples: A: 적립해 드릴까요? / B: 네, 적립해 주세요.
A: Shall I add your points? / B: Yes, please.
Staff proactively offer with 드릴까요; you confirm with 주세요 — the most common exchange at any chain store
적립해 주세요. 전화번호로요.
Add my points, please. By phone number.
전화번호로요 = 'by (my) phone number'; most Korean stores track points via your mobile number, not a physical card
계산하기 전에 적립 먼저 해 주세요. 010-1234-5678이요.
Before you ring it up, please add my points first. It's 010-1234-5678.
Real flow: say 먼저 (first) before payment is charged, then read your number — timing matters because some systems can't add points after payment
nuance: 적립 (積立) means 'accumulating/saving up,' and 적립해 주세요 asks the cashier to credit loyalty points or stamps to your account — via phone number, an app barcode, or a membership card. This is customer-to-staff, plain polite -요; 반말 (적립해 줘) is friends-only. Say it before payment, because most POS systems cannot retroactively add points. The nearest alternatives are 적립 부탁드려요 (more deferential, very polite) and the ultra-casual 적립이요 while showing your barcode — all mean the same thing, divided only by politeness level. A frequent English-speaker mistake is 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather points') — Koreans do not phrase it that way; the correct verb is 적립하다. Also critical: 적립 is earning points; spending them is entirely different — you would say 포인트로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요 to redeem.

structuredNuance.t: 적립해(accumulate/save up + verb ending) + 주세요(please give/do for me). Literally 'please do the accumulation for me' — really 'please add loyalty points to my account.' 적립하다 is the specific verb for accruing points or savings; you cannot substitute 모으다 or 쌓다 at the counter.

Say this at checkout in any store that runs a loyalty program — coffee chains, convenience stores, pharmacies, bookstores. Say it before payment. Plain polite -요 for all staff; 반말 only with friends. If you forgot, you can try 혹시 아까 적립 됐어요? ('was it added just now?') but there is no guarantee.

적립 부탁드려요 is the most deferential form (appropriate when speaking to an elder or in a high-end shop). 적립이요 (bare noun + polite marker) is quick and very casual but acceptable at chains. The line: 적립해 주세요 → polite everyday; 부탁드려요 → deferential; 적립이요 → casual shorthand.

적립 (積立): 積 = accumulate/pile up + 立 = stand/establish. The compound means 'building up a store of something' — hence the loyalty-points meaning. Same 積 appears in 축적하다 (accumulate) and 적금 (installment savings account).

Do not say 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather my points') — unnatural; the verb must be 적립하다. Also do not confuse earning (적립) with spending: to redeem points say 포인트로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요. Using 적립해 주세요 when you mean to pay with points confuses the staff.

mistakes: Saying 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather points') — not the natural phrasing; the correct verb for accruing loyalty points is 적립하다: 적립해 주세요.
Confusing earning with spending — 적립 is earning points; to redeem them say 포인트로 결제할게요 / 포인트 쓸게요.
Forgetting to provide your identifier — staff need your 전화번호, app barcode, or membership card; have it ready as you say 적립해 주세요, or add 전화번호로요 immediately after.

usage: Shall I give you a bag?
Cashier to customer; -ㄹ까요? is the polite service offer
Equally common staff version using 필요하다 (to need)
Shall I give you a bag separately?
Extension: 따로 = 'separately/on the side,' since bags are usually charged
examples: A: 봉투 드릴까요? / B: 네, 주세요.
A: Would you like a bag? / B: Yes, please.
Say 네 주세요 to accept, 아니요 괜찮아요 to decline — do not say 괜찮아요 alone thinking it means 'yes'
A: 봉투 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 주세요.
A: Need a bag? / B: No, just hand it over as-is.
그냥 주세요 = 'just give it to me (without a bag)'; a concise, polite way to decline
A: 봉투 드릴까요? 50원이에요. / B: 네, 하나 주세요.
A: Want a bag? It's 50 won. / B: Yes, one please.
Korean stores charge a small fee for bags by law; staff often state the price — expect it and answer 네, 하나 주세요
nuance: Since Korea mandates charges for single-use plastic bags, the cashier almost always asks 봉투 드릴까요? or 봉투 필요하세요? and will add a small fee (typically 20–50원). This phrase is staff-to-customer 존댓말 (드리다 humble 'give' + offer -ㄹ까요?); your job is just to answer. Accept with 네, 주세요 or 네, 하나 주세요; decline with 아니요, 괜찮아요 or 그냥 주세요. The near-synonym is 봉지 드릴까요? — 봉투 and 봉지 both mean 'bag' and are interchangeable in this context; the only difference is slight regional/speaker preference. The critical English-speaker trap is responding 괜찮아요 meaning 'okay yes I want one' — in Korean 괜찮아요 here means 'it's fine/no thanks,' so you would end up refusing the bag you actually wanted; say 네, 주세요 to accept.

structuredNuance.t: 봉투(bag) + 드릴까요(shall I give you — humble offer). Literally 'Shall I humbly give you a bag?' — really 'Would you like a bag?' It is a standard service offer, not a yes/no question about your feelings; answer with a direct 네 주세요 or 아니요 괜찮아요.

Heard at every checkout in Korea — supermarkets, convenience stores, bakeries, clothing stores. Bags are paid items. Staff use humble 드리다 toward you; you answer in plain -요. No need to match their formality level.
봉지 드릴까요? is fully interchangeable — 봉투 and 봉지 both mean a carry bag in this context. 봉투 필요하세요? is another common staff phrase ('Do you need a bag?') that calls for the same answer.
Accept: 네, 주세요 / 하나 주세요 / 큰 걸로 주세요 (large bag). Decline: 아니요, 괜찮아요 / 그냥 주세요 / 가방 있어요 (I have my own bag). If you need two: 두 개 주세요.
Answering 괜찮아요 meaning 'yes/sure' is the classic trap. In Korean 괜찮아요 ('it's fine/okay') in response to an offer means 'no thanks' — you will refuse the bag you wanted. To accept, always say 네, 주세요.

mistakes: Answering 괜찮아요 to mean 'yes, sure' — in Korean this declines the offer ('I'm fine without it'); to accept a bag say 네, 주세요.
Thinking bags are free — Korean stores charge for 봉투 by law; a small fee is added and the staff usually state the amount.
Treating 봉투 and 봉지 as different items — both mean 'shopping bag' in this context and are interchangeable; either form in the question gets the same answer.

usage: Customer requesting a bag at checkout; plain polite -요
Could you give me one bag?
Extension: specify size with 큰/작은 걸로
examples: 봉투 주세요.
A bag, please.
The direct request when staff did not proactively offer one — natural and polite
봉투 하나 주세요. 음료수가 많아서요.
One bag, please. I've got a lot of drinks.
-아서요 gives a soft reason; saying 하나 (one) avoids being handed several bags you do not need
A: 이거 다 못 들겠어요. / B: 봉투 두 개만 주세요.
A: I can't carry all this. / B: Just two bags, please.
두 개만 = 'just two'; -만 limits the number politely — useful when you need multiple bags
nuance: 봉투 주세요 is the customer-initiated request for a bag when staff did not first offer one. Plain polite -요 covers all store contexts; 반말 봉투 줘 is friends-only. To soften the request add 주시겠어요 (봉투 하나 주시겠어요?); to specify count or size tack them on (봉투 하나 / 큰 걸로). Remember bags are paid items, so saying 봉투 주세요 means you accept the small charge; don't be surprised when it appears on your total. The nearest alternative 봉지 주세요 is fully interchangeable. The classic English-speaker error is asking for 가방 — 가방 is a wearable bag like a backpack or purse, not a store shopping bag; the checkout carry-bag is 봉투 or 봉지. A secondary slip is responding to staff's 봉투 드릴까요? with a redundant full sentence 봉투 주세요; the natural accept is a simple 네, 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 봉투 (bag/envelope) + 주세요 (please give me). Literally 'please give me a bag.' 봉투 also means a paper envelope, but in a store context it always means the shopping carry-bag — context disambiguates instantly.
Use when the cashier did not ask first and you need a bag. Plain polite -요 is right for all staff. To be softer: 봉투 하나 주시겠어요? To be quicker: 봉투요. Never use 가방 주세요 — that asks for a handbag.

봉지 주세요 is fully interchangeable with 봉투 주세요 — both refer to the same disposable shopping bag. 봉투 주시겠어요? is the softened version for a more polite tone. The line between 봉투 and 봉지 is regional/personal preference, not meaning.
봉투 주세요 → 봉투 하나 주세요 (one bag) → 봉투 두 개 주세요 (two bags) → 봉투 큰 걸로 주세요 (large bag) → 봉투 주시겠어요? (extra-polite). Decline after staff offer: 아니요, 괜찮아요.

Asking for 가방 is the classic mistake — 가방 is a shoulder bag or backpack you own and wear; the disposable store bag is 봉투/봉지. Also, when staff offered first and you want to accept, just say 네, 주세요 rather than repeating 봉투 주세요 — the repeated full sentence can sound demanding.

mistakes: Asking for 가방 — that is a personal handbag or backpack; the checkout carry-bag is 봉투 (or 봉지), not 가방.
Forgetting the bag costs money — 봉투 주세요 implicitly accepts the fee; do not look surprised when it appears on your receipt.
Replying to a staff offer with a flat 봉투 주세요 — when staff already asked 봉투 드릴까요?, the natural accept is 네, 주세요, not a new full sentence.

english: Shall I heat it up for you?
usage: Convenience-store or café staff offering to microwave your food
반말; a friend offering, never staff
Shall I heat it for you?
Shorter spoken staff variant; 드려요? alone is a quick offer
Extension: naming the specific item (도시락 / 삼각김밥 / 만두 etc.)
examples: A: 데워 드릴까요? / B: 네, 데워 주세요.
A: Shall I heat it up? / B: Yes, please.
Staff offer with 드릴까요; you accept with 데워 주세요 — match verb: 데우다, not 끓이다 or 요리하다
A: 데워 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 주세요.
A: Want it heated? / B: No, as it is, thanks.
그냥 주세요 declines heating and takes it at room temperature — the softest refusal
이 도시락 데워 주세요. 한 2분 정도요.
Please heat this lunchbox. About two minutes or so.
한 ~ 정도요 = 'about ~'; you can suggest the microwave time — staff will usually decide themselves but appreciate the cue
nuance: At 편의점 (convenience stores) and some cafés, staff offer 데워 드릴까요? for ready-to-eat microwavable items — 도시락 lunchboxes, 삼각김밥 rice triangles, 컵라면 additions, 붕어빵-style pastries. 데우다 specifically means 'to warm up/reheat (food)' — it is the right verb for reheating in a microwave or warmer, distinct from 끓이다 (boil a liquid) or 굽다 (grill/bake). This phrase is staff 존댓말; you accept with 데워 주세요 or decline with 그냥 주세요 / 아니요, 괜찮아요. The near alternative is 따뜻하게 해 드릴까요? ('shall I make it warm for you?'), used loosely the same way; the dividing line is that 데우다 is specifically about reheating a pre-cooked food item, whereas 따뜻하게 하다 is vaguer. The English-speaker mistake is responding 뜨겁게 해 주세요 ('make it scalding hot') or 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — both are wrong registers; the only natural answer for reheating is 데워 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 데워 (reheat — verb stem of 데우다 + connective -아/어) + 드릴까요 (shall I give/do for you — humble offer). Literally 'Shall I humbly reheat it for you?' — really 'Shall I heat this up?' It is a convenience-store service offer for microwavable ready food.

Heard mainly at 편의점 (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven, Emart24) when you pick up a 도시락, 삼각김밥, 만두, or any microwavable item. Staff use 존댓말 (드리다); you answer in plain -요. It is always a friendly low-pressure offer — declining with 그냥 주세요 is perfectly normal.
따뜻하게 해 드릴까요? is the looser alternative; 데워 드릴까요? is the more precise phrasing specific to reheating food (not warming a drink). 끓여 드릴까요? would mean boiling a liquid — not used for lunchboxes.
Accept: 데워 주세요 / 네, 부탁드려요. Decline: 그냥 주세요 / 아니요, 괜찮아요. Request specific time: 2분만 해 주세요 (just 2 minutes). Ask yourself: 전자레인지 어디 있어요? (if you want to use the store microwave yourself).

Do not say 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — that implies raw ingredients; ready food is simply 데워 주세요. Also do not say 뜨겁게 해 주세요 for reheating — that means 'make it dangerously hot'; the correct, natural word for warming food is 데우다.

mistakes: Using 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — that asks for fresh cooking from raw ingredients; reheating ready food is 데워 주세요.
Saying 끓여 주세요 ('boil it') for a lunchbox — 끓이다 is for liquids; microwaving solid food is 데우다.
Declining with a blunt 아니요 only — soften it to 아니요, 그냥 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요 to avoid sounding rude.

usage: Café staff to customer; 드시고 가다 = eat/drink here, 가져가다 = take away
반말; only between friends, not said by staff
More formal/standard register; 포장 = packed to go
Extension: asks only about the dine-in half, expecting a yes/no
examples: A: 드시고 가세요, 가져가세요? / B: 가져갈게요.
A: For here or to go? / B: To go.
가져갈게요 is the cleanest takeout answer; 포장이요 or 포장해 주세요 also work — choose any
A: 드시고 가세요? / B: 네, 여기서 먹고 갈게요.
A: Eating in? / B: Yes, I'll have it here.
Dine-in answer: 여기서 먹고 갈게요; note you use plain 먹다 about yourself, not the honorific 드시다 the staff used
A: 드시고 가세요, 가져가세요? / B: 포장해 주세요. 따로 담아 주시고요.
A: For here or to go? / B: To go please. And could you pack them separately?
따로 담아 주시고요 = 'pack them in separate containers'; -고요 adds a second request naturally after the main one
nuance: This is the café's dine-in-versus-takeout question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다/마시다, so 드시고 가세요? = 'will you eat/drink here and go?'; 가져가세요? = 'will you take it away?' The question matters practically: Korean law requires cafés to serve dine-in orders in reusable mugs/glasses, while takeout uses disposables — so your answer changes the cup you receive. Staff use 존댓말 with the honorific 드시다; you answer in plain polite -요 using your own 먹다/마시다: 먹고 갈게요 (dine in) or 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요 (takeout). The more formal phrasing is 매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요?. The English-speaker error is replying 테이크아웃 — understood but unnatural; say 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. Another trap is reversing the honorific: don't say 드시고 갈게요 about yourself — reserve 드시다 for talking about others; use 먹고/마시고 for yourself.

structuredNuance.t: 드시고 가세요 = 'will you eat (honorific) and go?' + 가져가세요 = 'will you take (it) away?' Together they form the binary for-here-or-to-go question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다/마시다, used by staff to honor the customer — do not use 드시다 about yourself in your answer.

Heard at every café and many bakeries in Korea. Your answer changes the cup and packaging. Staff always use 존댓말 and honorific 드시다; you reply with plain polite -요 using 먹다 or 마시다 about yourself. Never say 드시고 갈게요 about yourself.

매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요? is the same question in slightly more formal dress, heard at restaurants. 여기서 드실 거예요? asks the dine-in half only. All call for the same answers: 먹고 갈게요 (stay) / 포장이요, 가져갈게요, 포장해 주세요 (go).
Dine-in answers: 먹고 갈게요 / 여기서 마실게요 / 네, 드시고 갈게요 (wrong — don't use 드시다 about yourself; say 먹고 갈게요). Takeout answers: 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요.

Saying 테이크아웃 is understood but marked as a loanword answer; the natural answers are 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. The grammar trap: staff say 드시고 가세요? using the honorific; do NOT reply 드시고 갈게요 — 드시다 is only for talking about other people. Use 먹고 갈게요 about yourself.

mistakes: Answering with English 테이크아웃 or just 고 — say 포장이요 / 가져갈게요 / 포장해 주세요 instead.
Saying 드시고 갈게요 about yourself — 드시다 is the honorific for talking about others; use 먹고 갈게요 / 마시고 갈게요 for yourself.
Assuming dine-in and takeout cups are the same — Korean law requires real mugs for dine-in; your answer changes the cup you receive.

usage: Customer asking for a to-go paper/plastic cup even while staying in
Put it in a paper cup.
반말; friends only, not for staff
Common loanword variant; same meaning and widely understood
Please put it in a disposable cup.
Extension with 담다 ('to fill/pour into'), a touch more precise and polite
examples: A: 머그잔에 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 일회용 컵에 주세요.
A: In a mug? / B: No, a disposable cup please.
Used to override the default dine-in mug — the explicit contrast 머그잔 vs 일회용 컵 makes your preference unmistakable
여기서 마실 건데 일회용 컵에 주세요. 곧 나가야 해서요.
I'll drink here but in a disposable cup, please. I have to leave soon.
-ㄹ 건데 = 'I'm going to ~ but'; giving a reason (곧 나가야 해서) makes the unusual request more natural and reduces any awkwardness
일회용 컵에 주시고, 캐리어도 하나 주세요.
A disposable cup, please, and a cup carrier too.
캐리어 = drink carrier tray; 주시고 chains the second request after the first smoothly
nuance: 일회용 (一回用) means 'single-use', and 일회용 컵 is a disposable paper or plastic cup. You need this phrase in Korea because cafés are legally required to serve dine-in customers in real mugs or glasses — if you want a to-go cup even while sitting, you must ask explicitly. Customer-to-staff plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only. The everyday alternative is 테이크아웃 컵에 주세요 — fully interchangeable and understood at all chains; 종이컵에 주세요 is more specific if it is definitely a paper cup. The particle -에 is critical: it marks destination or container ('into the ~') — not -로 (which would change meaning). The English-speaker mistake is either saying 일회용 잔 (잔 is glassware: wine glass, mug) or omitting the particle and saying just 일회용 컵 주세요, which sounds like you want the cup handed to you empty rather than your drink poured into it.

structuredNuance.t: 일회용(single-use) + 컵(cup) + 에(into/destination particle) + 주세요(please give me). Literally 'please give me [the drink] into a disposable cup.' The particle -에 marks where the drink goes — it is not 일회용 컵을 주세요 (which would ask for an empty cup).

Used when dining in at a café but wanting a to-go cup — because you're leaving soon, or just prefer it. Since Korean law defaults to mugs/glasses for dine-in, you must actively request this. Plain -요 polite to staff; 반말 only with friends.
테이크아웃 컵에 주세요 is interchangeable. 종이컵에 주세요 specifies paper specifically. 플라스틱 컵에 주세요 is technically correct but stilted — 일회용 컵 or 테이크아웃 컵 sounds more natural.
일회용 (一回用): 一 = one + 回 = time/round + 用 = use. 'Single-use' — the same 用 appears in 사용 (使用, use) and 용도 (用途, intended use). Do not confuse 일회용 (one-use) with 일회 (一回, one round/time) alone.
Saying 일회용 잔 is wrong — 잔 refers to glassware and ceramicware (와인 잔, 머그잔); disposables use 컵. Also do not say 플라스틱 컵 directly — understood but stiff. The correct choice is 일회용 컵 or 테이크아웃 컵.

mistakes: Saying 일회용 잔 — 잔 implies glass or ceramic ware; disposable cups take the word 컵: 일회용 컵에 주세요.
Assuming dine-in automatically means a paper cup — Korean cafés give real mugs for here by law; you must request 일회용 컵 explicitly.
Using 플라스틱 컵에 주세요 woodenly — understood but stiff; 일회용 컵에 주세요 or 테이크아웃 컵에 주세요 sounds natural and confident.

english: Please put it in my tumbler
usage: Customer handing a personal cup to the barista; 담다 = to fill/pour into
Looser spoken variant; 해 주세요 stands in for 담아 주세요 colloquially
I brought a tumbler — please fill this one.
Extension: announce you have a tumbler first, then point and ask; lets staff apply the discount
examples: A: 텀블러에 담아 주세요. / B: 네, 할인 들어가세요.
A: In my tumbler, please. / B: Sure, your discount will be applied.
Bringing a personal cup usually earns a 텀블러 할인 (around 300–500원 discount) at most chains — announce it early
이 텀블러 깨끗해요. 여기에 담아 주세요.
This tumbler is clean. Please fill it here.
Reassuring the barista it is clean is polite and practical; 여기에 (여기 + destination -에) = 'in here/into this'
아이스 아메리카노 텀블러에 담아 주세요. 얼음 따로 주시고요.
An iced americano in my tumbler, please. And the ice separately.
얼음 따로 = ice on the side (useful when your tumbler cannot hold both drink and full ice); 주시고요 chains the second request
nuance: 텀블러 (tumbler) is a reusable personal cup, and 텀블러에 담아 주세요 hands it to the barista with a request to fill it. 담다 ('to pour/fill into a container') is the precise verb here — it emphasizes putting liquid into the vessel, making it more natural than the generic 넣어 주세요. The destination particle -에 marks where the drink goes (텀블러에 = 'into the tumbler'); using -로 instead (텀블러로 주세요) shifts meaning to 'give me a tumbler as the item,' which is wrong. Bringing a tumbler typically earns a discount (텀블러 할인) at Korean café chains, so announce it early. The loose spoken alternative is 텀블러에 해 주세요. A refill situation calls for 채워 주세요 ('fill it up'), but for a fresh drink 담아 주세요 is the correct natural form.

structuredNuance.t: 텀블러에 (into the tumbler — -에 marks destination) + 담아 (fill/pour in — verb 담다 + connective) + 주세요 (please). Literally 'please fill/pour into my tumbler.' The verb 담다 specifically conveys pouring a liquid into a container — it is more precise than 넣다 (to insert/put in, for solid objects).

Hand over your tumbler as you order and say this phrase. Works at all café chains and independent cafés. Earns a discount (텀블러 할인) at most chains. Plain -요 polite for all staff; 반말 with friends. Announce it before the barista starts making the drink.

텀블러에 해 주세요 is the lazy but acceptable spoken shorthand. 채워 주세요 ('fill it up') suits a refill but sounds odd for a fresh drink. 넣어 주세요 ('put it in') is for solid objects — wrong for a liquid poured into a cup; use 담다 for drinks.
Basic: 텀블러에 담아 주세요. With announcement: 텀블러 가져왔어요, 여기에 담아 주세요. Refill: 텀블러 채워 주세요 (fill it up again). Confirming discount: 텀블러 할인 되나요?

Using -로 instead of -에 is the main particle mistake: 텀블러로 주세요 means 'give me a tumbler (as the product),' not 'pour into my tumbler.' For any container you are filling, the destination particle is -에. Also, 넣어 주세요 sounds like putting a solid object in; the right verb for pouring a drink is 담다.

mistakes: Saying 텀블러로 주세요 — -로 marks the item being given ('give me a tumbler'); to fill your cup use the destination particle -에: 텀블러에 담아 주세요.
Using 넣어 주세요 ('insert it') — 넣다 is for placing solid objects; pouring a drink into a cup is 담다.
Forgetting to announce the tumbler before ordering — say 텀블러 가져왔어요 first so the barista can apply the discount and prepare the right size.

usage: The standard polite price question to any shop staff
반말; to a friend or a very familiar person
Softer, slightly more polite and indirect variant
Extension: point with 이거 ('this one') at the specific item
examples: A: 얼마예요? / B: 4,500원입니다.
A: How much is it? / B: It's 4,500 won.
Staff answer with 원입니다; the bare question works anywhere — no subject needed because the item is understood from context
이 빵 얼마예요? 가격표가 없네요.
How much is this bread? There's no price tag.
-네요 expresses a fresh observation ('I notice there's no tag'); 이 빵 names the item you're asking about
다 해서 얼마예요? 카드 돼요?
How much all together? Do you take card?
다 해서 = 'all in, total'; a natural two-question checkout combo — ask total then payment method
nuance: 얼마예요? is one of the first and most essential phrases for any Korean learner — the everyday polite 'how much?' for any purchase. 얼마 = 'how much / how many (price-related)' + 예요 the polite copula. Plain -요 covers every store, market, and taxi; 반말 얼마야? is for friends. Softer is 얼마인가요? (indirect, slightly more formal). For a total: 다 해서 얼마예요? The dividing line between 얼마예요? and 얼마인가요? is degree of indirectness — same meaning. The top English-speaker spelling mistake is writing 얼마에요 — after the vowel-final word 얼마, the polite copula must be 예요, not 에요 (얼마에요 is a common but wrong romanization habit). A semantic trap: 얼마 있어요? means 'how much (money) do you have?' — not 'how much does it cost'; always use 얼마예요? for price. Korean prices use 만 (10,000) and 천 (1,000) units, so train your ear: 사천오백 = 4,500, 일만 이천 = 12,000.

structuredNuance.t: 얼마(how much/many — price) + 예요(polite copula 'is'). Literally 'How much is it?' — exactly what it says. The subject (the item) is dropped because it is understood; this short question works at any counter with no additional context.

Appropriate everywhere: cafés, markets, taxis, clothing stores, pharmacies. -요 polite for strangers and staff; 반말 얼마야? only with close friends. Pointing at the item while asking (이거 얼마예요?) avoids any ambiguity.

얼마인가요? is the indirect, slightly more formal version — same meaning but sounds less blunt. 가격이 어떻게 돼요? ('what is the price?') is a wordy alternative heard at fancier shops. For the total: 다 해서 얼마예요? is the standard checkout phrase.
얼마예요? → 이거 얼마예요? (point at item) → 다 해서 얼마예요? (total) → 할인되나요? (any discount?). 반말: 얼마야? Formal: 얼마인가요?
Writing 얼마에요 is the top spelling mistake — after the vowel-final 얼마 the copula is 예요, not 에요. Also do not say 얼마 있어요? for a price — that asks how much money you possess; the price question is 얼마예요?.

mistakes: Spelling it 얼마에요 — after vowel-final 얼마 the polite copula is 예요, not 에요: correct form is 얼마예요.
Saying 얼마 있어요? to ask a price — that asks how much money someone has; the cost question is 얼마예요?.
Expecting digit-by-digit prices — Koreans use 만/천/백 units (사천오백 원 = 4,500 won); train your ear for these chunked number units.

usage: Customer stating payment method; -ㄹ게요 = 'I'll (do)' — declares the speaker's decision
More formal -겠습니다; in a corporate or very formal setting
Extension with 계산하다 ('to settle/pay'), fully natural and interchangeable
examples: A: 현금이세요, 카드세요? / B: 카드로 할게요.
A: Cash or card? / B: Card, please.
-로 marks the method (instrument); -ㄹ게요 is the speaker's own decision — do not say 카드로 할 거예요 (that would describe a plan, not commit here)
카드로 할게요. 일시불로요.
By card, please. Lump-sum payment.
일시불 = single full payment (vs 할부 = installments); for everyday purchases always answer 일시불로요 unless splitting
A: 카드로 할게요. 여기 찍으면 돼요? / B: 네, 여기에 태그해 주세요.
A: I'll pay by card. Do I tap here? / B: Yes, tap here please.
찍다 / 태그하다 = tap/tap for contactless; asking where the reader is is practical in smaller shops without clear signage
nuance: 카드로 할게요 tells the cashier you are paying by card; -로 marks the means or instrument ('by way of card') and -ㄹ게요 announces a decision you are committing to right now. Plain polite -요 for all stores; formal -하겠습니다 in rare stiff contexts; 반말 with close friends. After you say it, staff may ask 일시불이세요, 할부세요? (one lump payment or installments?) — for any everyday purchase answer 일시불로요. The near alternative is 카드로 계산할게요 (identical meaning, slightly more explicit) or 카드 될까요? (asking whether card is accepted — a question, not a statement). The dividing line: 할게요 commits to paying by card; 될까요? merely inquires. The English-speaker mistake is 카드로 지불할게요 — 지불하다 is the correct Sino-Korean verb for 'to pay' but it is bookish and stiff in conversation; spoken Korean uses 하다 or 계산하다. The wrong particle is also common: payment method takes -로 (instrument), not -를 or -에.

structuredNuance.t: 카드(card) + 로(instrument particle, 'by means of') + 할게요(I'll do it — volitional -ㄹ게요). Literally 'I'll do it by card' — really 'I'll pay by card.' The -ㄹ게요 ending signals a self-directed decision being announced to the listener, not a plan or a question.

Said at any checkout when you want to pay by card, either when staff ask or proactively. Plain -요 for all stores; formal -하겠습니다 in a business/formal setting; 반말 with close friends. Be ready to answer 일시불이세요, 할부세요? immediately after.

카드로 계산할게요 is fully interchangeable and slightly more explicit. 카드 될까요? asks if card is accepted (a question). 카드로 하겠습니다 is the formal version. The line: 할게요/계산할게요 = committing to card; 될까요? = asking permission.
카드로 할게요 → 카드로 계산할게요 → 카드로 하겠습니다 (formal). Installment: 할부로 해 주세요 / 3개월 할부로요. Lump-sum: 일시불로요. Inquiry: 카드 돼요? / 카드 되나요?

카드로 지불할게요 is grammatically fine but sounds written and stiff — spoken Korean says 카드로 할게요 or 카드로 계산할게요. Wrong-particle error: 카드를 할게요 or 카드에 할게요 are both wrong; payment method takes -로 (instrument particle).

mistakes: Using 지불하다 (카드로 지불할게요) — grammatically correct but stiff and written; say 카드로 할게요 or 카드로 계산할게요 in conversation.
Wrong particle: 카드를 할게요 or 카드에 할게요 — payment method takes the instrument particle -로: 카드로.
Freezing when asked 일시불이세요, 할부세요? — for everyday purchases just say 일시불로요 (one full payment); only ask for 할부 if you want monthly installments.

english: Please give me a cash receipt
usage: Customer paying cash and requesting a tax-linked receipt for year-end deduction
More formal/precise with 발급하다 ('to issue officially')
A cash receipt to my phone number, please.
Extension: specify that your number should be used as the identifier
examples: A: 현금영수증 해 드릴까요? / B: 네, 해 주세요.
A: Shall I issue a cash receipt? / B: Yes, please.
Staff proactively offer; you confirm with 해 주세요 — have your phone number ready immediately
현금으로 할게요. 현금영수증 해 주세요. 010-1234-5678이요.
I'll pay cash. And a cash receipt, please. It's 010-1234-5678.
Real flow: state cash payment → request receipt → read your number, all in one smooth turn
현금영수증 소득공제로 해 주세요.
Please register the receipt for income deduction.
소득공제용 (personal income deduction) vs 지출증빙용 (business expense proof) — most individuals say 소득공제로요
nuance: 현금영수증 (現金領收證) is a uniquely Korean institution: a cash receipt registered to your phone number or resident registration number so that it counts toward your annual income tax deduction. Unlike a regular 영수증 (printed slip), this one is electronically submitted to the National Tax Service automatically. 해 주세요 ('please do/issue it') is the everyday request; 발급해 주세요 is the formal verb. Plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only. Staff may follow with 소득공제용이세요, 지출증빙용이세요? — for personal use say 소득공제로요; for a business expense 지출증빙으로요. The critical near-synonym comparison: 영수증 주세요 just asks for the printed paper receipt with no tax link. The English-speaker mistake is asking only for 영수증 and missing the tax benefit altogether, or trying to request it on a card payment — 현금영수증 applies exclusively to 현금 (cash); cards automatically record their own transactions.

structuredNuance.t: 현금(cash) + 영수증(receipt) + 해 주세요(please do/issue). Literally 'please do the cash receipt' — really 'please register this cash purchase for my tax deduction.' It is not just a paper receipt; it links to your ID for year-end tax benefits.

Say this whenever you pay cash at any store. Must be done at the time of payment — you cannot add it retroactively in most systems. Plain -요 polite to staff. Have your 휴대폰 번호 (mobile number) ready; some stores accept your resident registration number instead.

영수증 주세요 is a plain printed receipt — no tax link. 현금영수증 해 주세요 is the tax-registered receipt. 현금영수증 발급해 주세요 is the formal version. The key dividing line: 영수증 is just proof of purchase; 현금영수증 is linked to the national tax system.
현금영수증 (現金領收證): 現金 = cash + 領收 = receive/collect + 證 = certificate/proof. The 領收證 part is the same 영수증 (receipt). Same 現金 appears in 현금 인출기 (ATM, cash withdrawal machine).

Asking for just 영수증 misses the tax benefit — you only get a paper slip, not the tax-registered receipt. Also do not request 현금영수증 after paying by card — it only applies to cash payments; cards automatically register their own transactions.

mistakes: Asking for plain 영수증 expecting the tax benefit — that only gets you a printed slip; the tax-registered version is 현금영수증 해 주세요.
Requesting it on a card payment — 현금영수증 is for 현금 (cash) only; card payments are automatically recorded separately.
Forgetting to give your phone number — the receipt registers to your 휴대폰 번호, so read it out immediately after the request: 010-XXXX-XXXX이요.

usage: Customer asking staff or looking around for the self-serve straw station
Extension: skip location-finding and just ask staff to hand you one
examples: A: 빨대 어디 있어요? / B: 저쪽 셀프바에 있어요.
A: Where are the straws? / B: Over at the self-serve bar.
셀프바 (self-serve bar) is where most Korean cafés keep straws, lids, napkins, sugar, and water; 저쪽 = 'over there'
빨대 어디 있어요? 안 보여서요.
Where are the straws? I can't find them.
안 보여서요 = 'because I can't see them' — a natural soft reason added with -서요 to soften the request and explain why you're asking
빨대랑 냅킨 어디 있어요?
Where are the straws and napkins?
랑 links two items naturally in speech; 냅킨 (napkin) or 휴지 are usually at the same 셀프바 as straws
nuance: Most Korean cafés organize a 셀프바 (self-serve station) with straws, lids, sugar, creamers, napkins, and water, so 빨대 어디 있어요? is the practical question when you cannot locate it. 빨대 means 'straw' (literally 'sucking stick,' from the verb 빨다 'to suck'). 어디 있어요? = 'where is it?' using the existence/location verb 있다. Plain polite -요 to staff; 반말 어디 있어? with friends. If you prefer not to go find it yourself, substitute 빨대 좀 주세요 (please hand me one) — the dividing line is self-serve vs staff-fetched. Note paper straws (종이 빨대) are now standard at many Korean cafés due to environmental regulations. The English-speaker mistake is the verb choice: 빨대 어디예요? uses the copula 이다 to ask 'where is it (as a place)?' — grammatically this sounds like asking where the straw is as a location/address. Object location uses 있다: 빨대 어디 있어요? Another slip is calling it a 스트로 — the native word 빨대 is what Koreans say.

structuredNuance.t: 빨대(straw) + 어디(where) + 있어요(is/exists — location verb). Literally 'Where does the straw exist?' — naturally 'Where are the straws?' The verb 있다 (to exist/be at) is essential for locating objects; do not use 이다 (to be/equal) as 어디예요?.

Directed at any café staff or used while looking around. Most straws are at the 셀프바 — a quick point from staff is the usual answer. Plain -요 polite; 반말 어디 있어? with friends. To avoid the location search entirely: 빨대 좀 주세요.
빨대 좀 주세요 ('please hand me a straw') skips finding it yourself — the dividing line is whether you fetch it or staff bring it. 빨대 어디에 있나요? is the softened indirect form, slightly more formal.
빨대 어디 있어요? → 빨대 어디에 있나요? (softer) → 종이 빨대 있어요? (paper straws available?) → 빨대 좀 주세요 (just give me one). Add an item: 빨대랑 냅킨 어디 있어요?

빨대 어디예요? uses 이다 (copula), which sounds like asking the straw's location as an address — awkward for an object. For locating things use 있다: 빨대 어디 있어요?. Also avoid 스트로 — the everyday Korean word is 빨대.

mistakes: Saying 빨대 어디예요? — for object location use 있어요? (existence verb): 빨대 어디 있어요?; 어디예요? asks where a place is, not where an object is.
Calling it 스트로 — the everyday Korean word is 빨대; 스트로 sounds unnatural and foreign.
Expecting staff to bring it unasked — straws are self-serve at the 셀프바 in most Korean cafés; either locate the station or explicitly say 빨대 좀 주세요.

usage: Customer asking staff or checking a specific spot at a café or restaurant
Are there seats, by any chance?
Is there a table for two?
Extension: state party size with 명 to get a more useful answer
examples: A: 자리 있어요? / B: 네, 2층에 있어요.
A: Any seats? / B: Yes, there are some upstairs on the 2nd floor.
Korean cafés often direct you to a floor rather than personally seating you — listen for 층 (floor) cues and go yourself
혹시 자리 있어요? 콘센트 있는 자리면 좋겠어요.
Any seats by any chance? Preferably a spot with a power outlet.
혹시 softens the ask and implies 'I'm not sure but hoping'; 콘센트 있는 자리 = seat with an electrical outlet, important for café work
지금 자리 있어요? 두 명인데요.
Any seats right now? There are two of us.
-인데요 adds context (party size of two) and invites the staff to respond with the most useful information, not just yes/no
nuance: 자리 있어요? asks whether a seat or spot is free — at a busy café, at a restaurant entrance, or directly to a person whose nearby seat appears empty. 자리 = 'seat, spot, place'. Plain polite -요; 반말 자리 있어? with friends; softened 자리 있나요?. Add 혹시 before the question to sound less demanding, or state party size (두 명 자리 있어요?) for a more useful reply from staff. The near alternative is 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') — the dividing line is scope: 자리 있어요? asks about general availability anywhere in the venue, while 앉아도 돼요? asks permission for one specific seat you're standing next to. For written or formal contexts (reserved seating, cinema) the more formal word 좌석 is used; in a café the natural word is always 자리. Also note 자리를 잡다 ('to claim/save a seat') is a separate phrase — 자리 있어요? only asks about availability.

structuredNuance.t: 자리(seat/spot) + 있어요?(is there/are there — existence verb). Literally 'Is there a seat/spot?' — really 'Are there any seats available?' The existence verb 있다 is critical for availability questions about objects and places.

Use at café entrances, to staff at restaurants, or to a stranger sitting near an empty adjacent seat. Plain -요 polite; 반말 with friends; 혹시 자리 있나요? for extra softness. Korean cafés often do not seat you — they answer and expect you to walk over.

여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') is specific to one seat you're pointing at, while 자리 있어요? asks about any available seat in the whole venue. 좌석 있어요? is the formal/written version (theater, ticketed seating) — in a café it sounds too stiff; use 자리.
자리 있어요? → 혹시 자리 있어요? (softer) → 두/세 명 자리 있어요? (party size) → 콘센트 있는 자리 있어요? (outlet seat) → 창가 자리 있어요? (window seat). Formal: 자리 있나요?

자리예요? uses the copula 이다 and asks 'what is this, a seat?' — nonsensical for availability. Availability questions use the existence verb 있다: 자리 있어요?. Also do not use 좌석 in a casual café — 좌석 is formal/written (cinema, plane seat numbers); 자리 is the everyday word.

mistakes: Saying 자리예요? for availability — use the existence verb 있어요?: 자리 있어요?; 자리예요? would sound like 'is this a seat?'
Using 좌석 in a casual café — 좌석 is the formal/written term (cinema, reserved seating); in everyday café speech the word is 자리.
Asking 자리 있어요? when you mean a specific empty seat right next to you — for that, ask 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') instead.

english: To go, please / Pack it up
usage: Customer choosing takeout; 포장 = packing/wrapping to take away
Clipped one-word answer to the dine-in-or-takeout question
Can I get this to go?
Extension: ask first whether takeout is possible for this particular item
examples: A: 드시고 가세요? / B: 아니요, 포장해 주세요.
A: Eating in? / B: No, to go please.
The natural takeout answer to the dine-in-or-to-go question; 포장해 주세요 tells staff to pack it, not just that you're leaving
라떼 한 잔 포장해 주세요. 캐리어도 주시고요.
One latte to go, please. A carrier too.
캐리어 = the cardboard or plastic drink carrier; 주시고요 chains a second request after the main one — natural at a busy counter
남은 거 포장해 주세요. 집에서 먹을게요.
Please pack up the leftovers. I'll eat them at home.
남은 거 = 'the leftovers'; 포장하다 works for restaurant doggy-bags too — the same phrase covers café takeout and restaurant leftovers
nuance: 포장해 주세요 is the all-purpose 'to go' or 'pack it up' request — for a café drink ordered fresh, a bakery item, or restaurant leftovers. 포장 (包裝) literally means 'wrapping/packaging.' Plain polite -요 for all staff; the even shorter clipped form 포장이요 works as a quick answer to a binary dine-in question; 반말 포장해 줘 is friends-only. The near alternative is 가져갈게요 ('I'll take it away') — the dividing line is who does the action: 포장해 주세요 asks staff to actively pack the item, while 가져갈게요 simply announces you're taking it; in practice both achieve takeout but 포장해 주세요 is more specific. Another alternative is 싸 주세요 ('wrap it up') — homey and natural for restaurant leftovers but slightly informal for a fresh café order. The English-speaker mistake is defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood at chains but 포장 is the fully native word, and 테이크아웃 컵 refers specifically to the cup type, not the whole transaction.

structuredNuance.t: 포장해(pack/wrap — verb 포장하다 + connective) + 주세요(please do for me). Literally 'please do the packaging for me' — really 'to go, please' or 'pack it up.' It covers both fresh café orders and restaurant doggy-bags.

Use at cafés when answering for-here-or-to-go, at bakeries, at restaurants to box leftovers. Plain -요 polite; clipped 포장이요 is even quicker; 반말 포장해 줘 with friends. Works for drinks, pastries, and restaurant food alike.

가져갈게요 ('I'll take it away') states your action but does not ask staff to pack anything — both mean takeout but 포장해 주세요 is the explicit pack-it-up request. 싸 주세요 ('wrap it') is homey/informal, natural for restaurant leftovers but slightly casual for a café. 테이크아웃 해 주세요 is understood at chains but 포장 is the fully native word.

포장 (包裝): 包 = wrap/envelop + 裝 = pack/outfit. Literally 'wrapping and packing.' The same 包 appears in 포함 (包含, inclusion) and 포기 has different characters. 포장도로 (paved road) uses 鋪裝, different 포 — do not confuse them.

Saying 테이크아웃 해 주세요 is understood but marks the loanword answer; the natural Korean is 포장해 주세요. Do not confuse 포장 (to-go packaging) with 선물 포장 (gift wrapping) — if you want gift wrap, specify: 선물 포장해 주세요.

mistakes: Defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood but the natural, fully Korean word is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Confusing 포장해 주세요 with dine-in — 포장해 주세요 is the takeout request; to eat in say 먹고 갈게요 or 여기서 먹을게요.
Using 포장 when you mean gift wrapping — in a café 포장 means 'pack to go'; for gift wrap specify 선물 포장해 주세요 so staff know the difference.
